techTree.title: Tech tree
techTree.intro: Every building, and what each of its levels costs, produces, and requires.

lore.longhouse: The heart of the settlement. Its level sets the claim radius, the build slots and which buildings unlock, and it produces a little of every resource and adds storage of its own. Every settlement starts with one, standing on grass.
lore.lumberjack: Fells timber on forested ground — the wood behind every wall and roof.
lore.quarry: Cuts stone from a mountain ridge — the bones of every keep.
lore.odinstatue: Odin's statue on grass, at Longhouse 25 behind a level-10 Druid Hut. Wisdom: every build in this settlement takes 2% less time per level (10% at level 5). Ravens: its claim, its towers and its armies see 2 more rings per level (10 at level 5). Counts as the settlement's one shrine.
lore.palisade: One hex of the settlement's wall, on grass, forest or sand inside its claim, from Longhouse 7 behind a level-5 Tower (the Palisade and its Gate share one tech-tree card). Walls never branch: no hex may end up with three wall neighbours. Which piece draws, a straight, a bend or an end, follows the neighbouring wall hexes. Every wall hex stops every land army, its owner's included; a lone end of a wall (one wall neighbour) is only half open, any army crosses it, only slower, unless it touches a mountain or a wide river. At the coast the wall ends on a shallow-water hex, the sea end, which stays sea. A won siege that targets a wall hex takes one level off it, however many catapults survive; fire will too, later.
lore.palisadegate: A wall hex with a gate, only where the wall runs straight between two opposite wall hexes. Its owner's armies and their friends' (the same guild, or a guild at peace with it) pass it as quickly as the ground under it; every other army is stopped like at any wall hex. Same unlock, prerequisite, levels and cost as the Palisade, on one tech-tree card.
lore.bridge: Opens a wide river to land armies. A causeway first, then a footbridge, the king's bridge, and a guarded bridge with forts that only you and your friends may cross. Attackers burn a guarded bridge down a level at a time.
lore.reindeerherder: A herder's hut and a pen of reindeer on open grassland — the settlement's first food building, available from the start.
lore.farm: Grows food on open grassland, keeping the longhouse table full. Buildable on every island, regardless of soil, from Longhouse 4 behind a level-3 Reindeer Herder (it and Pumpkin Farm share one tech-tree card).
lore.storagehouse: Extra room for the harvest, on grass. A resource stops being produced once it reaches the storage limit, so a full store wastes output.
lore.tower: A watch built on grass or sand at the border, pushing the claimed ground further out.
lore.fishinghut: A dock over shallow water, fishing the shallows a farm never could. It also stands on stilts on the half shore of a bog lake.
lore.pumpkinfarm: A second harvest for grass — pumpkins alongside the plain fields, yielding more than Farm. Only buildable on a Pumpkin-soil island (the game picks each island's soil, not the player) — the bonus crop a "more fertile" island unlocks.
lore.shrineofthor: Raised to Thor on grass, behind a level-5 Smithy — the war god's favour raises the attack of your land units (+10% at level 1, +22% at level 5). A settlement holds only one shrine in total, of any god, and each god has at most one shrine on an island.
lore.shrineoffreyja: Raised to Freyja on grass — its favour boosts Food production. A settlement holds only one shrine in total, of any god, and each god has at most one shrine on an island.
lore.shrineofullr: Raised to Ullr on grass — its favour boosts Wood production. A settlement holds only one shrine in total, of any god, and each god has at most one shrine on an island.
lore.shrineofnjord: Raised to Njörd on coastal water, behind a level-10 Dockyard — the sea god's favour raises the attack of your ships (+10% at level 1, +22% at level 5). A settlement holds only one shrine in total, of any god, and each god has at most one shrine on an island.
lore.archeryrange: Trains the land army's ranged specialists on grass or sand — bowmen, and once a Barracks-trained berserker line stands, catapults — in place of the longhouse.
lore.dockyard: Trains ships on shallow (coastal) water, in place of the longhouse.
lore.greatstorehouse: A late-game storage tier on grass, needing both the longhouse and this settlement's own storage house at level 15.
lore.barracks: Trains the land army's core line on grass or sand at the border — thralls, spearmen, axemen and berserkers — in place of the longhouse. Archery Range trains the rest of the roster (bowmen, catapults); the two never train the same unit.
lore.sawmill: Refines timber standing directly on a straight, gentle-bend, or tight-bend river tile — a waterwheel turning with the current, same as Crop Mill's. No Wood of its own: it boosts every Lumberjack within its level's range instead (a wider range and a bigger boost at higher levels).
lore.meadery: Keeps bees on grass behind a level-5 Farm — skeps, a honey press and a mead cellar. No effect of its own yet: the mead is meant for a future morale boost.
lore.townsquare: The village's own market square on grass — no effect of its own yet, but a future prerequisite or boost.
lore.cropmill: Grinds a level-10 Farm's grain on a straight river tile — a millstone under the open sky, its waterwheel turning with the current. No Food of its own: it boosts every Farm within its level's range instead (a wider range and a bigger boost at higher levels) — not Pumpkin Farm, a different crop a mill doesn't grind.
lore.smithy: The settlement's forge, with an anvil, on grass or sand behind a level-10 Barracks — the military line's capstone and the feeder of the Shrine of Thor. It produces nothing: it is where troops will be upgraded, a mechanic still to come.
lore.druidhut: A turf-roofed roundhouse on grass behind a Town Square, with a ring of runestones — no effect of its own yet, but meant for a future favour or rune mechanic.
lore.cartworkshop: Builds the settlement's carts on grass behind a Town Square — trains provisioners and settler crews in place of the longhouse. No storage of its own.
lore.claybrickworks: Digs and fires clay on bog moss — a pit, a drying rack and a kiln turning red earth into stone where no mountain stands.
lore.bogoreworks: The iron producer, on plain bog moss (not a shore, creek or lake): from a few diggings in the seeps to a bloomery smelting the ore. Every bog, creek or lake hex next to it adds 10% to its output, up to +50%.
lore.hammerschmiede: A water-powered hammer mill on a bog creek, behind a level-10 bog-ore works. No iron of its own: it raises every bog-ore works within its level's range instead (a wider range and a bigger boost at higher levels).

tiles.title: Tiles
tiles.intro: The terrain a world is made of, how it generates, and what can be built on it.
tiles.riverSawmillNote: The Sawmill is the one building that goes directly on a river tile — only a Straight or Bend one.

sea.title: Sea
sea.lore: Open water. Nothing stands on it, and nothing is grown or mined here — it only ever separates islands.
sea.generation: Every hex outside an island's radius.

coastalWater.title: Coastal water
coastalWater.lore: Still plain sea underneath — the same terrain as the open water beyond it — but close enough to the shore for a dock.
coastalWater.generation: A sea hex with at least one land neighbour: the ring hugging every island.

sand.title: Sand
sand.lore: An island's beach: the ring of land along its coast.
sand.generation: The outer edge of an island: beyond 82% of its radius from centre.

grass.title: Grass
grass.lore: Open lowland — most of a settlement is built here.
grass.generation: Lowland too smooth to be forest and too far from the centre to be mountain.

forest.title: Forest
forest.lore: Lowland gone rocky enough to grow trees instead of open grass.
forest.generation: Rockiness above the forest threshold, but not steep enough for mountain.

mountain.title: Mountain
mountain.lore: The rockiest ground an island has.
mountain.generation: Confined to an island's interior (within 40% of its radius) so ridges never form on the coast.

river.title: River
river.lore: Water cut through the land itself, from a mountain spring down to the sea — a river tile's art fully replaces whatever land terrain it flows over.
river.generation: Traced downhill from a spring on a qualifying mountain cluster (2+ connected mountain tiles) to the coast, meandering as it goes; two rivers that cross merge into a confluence, and anything shorter than 2 tiles is discarded.

impressum.title: Impressum
impressum.body: Bjarnøy is a hobby project built for the VanDooProject community. This placeholder page exists so the real landing page has somewhere to link to — replace it with your actual legal notice (operator, contact address, and any disclosures your jurisdiction requires) before going live.

wastedLands.title: The Wasted Lands
wastedLands.intro: Where the world ends. The Wasted Lands are a world's endgame: islands that rise from the sea when the giants wake, the fortress at the heart of them, and the last war the jarls of Bjarnøy fight.

lore.heading: The long winter's edge
lore.p1: The skalds say the sea around Bjarnøy was never empty. Past the last skerries, where the charts stop, lies Útgarðr: the Outyard, home of the Jötnar, the giants who were here before gods or men. For as long as the islands are young, the giants sleep, and the jarls fight each other for timber, stone and glory.
lore.p2: But every age grows old. When the halls are full and the runestones stand on every island, the giants wake. Out past the charted islands the sea boils, and new land rises from it: islands that were never green. On each of them smokes a fire-mountain, and on the greatest stands Utgard, a black citadel whose windows burn with cold rune-fire.
lore.p3: Nothing living has ever grown there. The ground is ash and cinder, the forests are bleached snags with their crowns snapped off, and the rivers run with fire. The beaches are black sand, and the sea around them is a sick green-black, choked around the wrecks of the longships that sailed too close to see what had risen. On the ridges, Jötun watchtowers keep the approaches, and Utgard's walls run from crag to shore.
lore.p4: No single jarl breaks Utgard. Its walls are built for a siege that lasts a generation, and the giants grow stronger while the jarls argue. Only guilds that sail as one host can storm the Outyard. Whoever throws down its gate ends the age, and their name is the last one carved before the world begins again.
lore.caption: This is how the endgame is meant to feel, not a rulebook. The mechanics are still being designed and may change.

utgard.heading: Utgard, the Outyard
utgard.body: A giant tile: one fortress over seven hexes, a basalt crag with a curtain wall, round towers and a central keep, lit from within by rune-fire and wrapped in mist.
utgard.techNote: The whole crag is cut into seven pieces, so each piece sorts on the map with the hex it stands on, like any other tile.

volcano.heading: The fire-mountain
volcano.body: The second giant of the Wasted Lands: a mountain that never cooled. Lava runs down its flanks, the crater bubbles and smoke rises from it without end. Like Utgard, it covers seven hexes.

defences.heading: Utgard's defences
defences.body: The giants don't leave their islands open. Jötun watchtowers guard the approaches, and walls in Utgard's own masonry close the ground between them, down to the waterline.

watchtower.heading: Jötun watchtower
watchtower.body: Utgard's answer to the jarls' towers: a round tower of dark coursed stone with rune-lit arrow slits. It rises in three stages, from scaffolding to a crowned top where the rune-fire burns in the open.

walls.heading: Utgard walls
walls.body: Battlemented curtain walls built from pieces that join edge to edge: straight runs, a gate, gentle and sharp bends, ends that finish on a tower, and ends that break off where they meet the sea.

endgame.heading: How the endgame plays
endgame.status: Planned: these rules are being built step by step and are not all in the game yet.
endgame.body: When the endboss rises, the wasted islands appear. Guilds wear down the jötnar together, hold their towers with armies, break Utgard's walls with siege engines and storm the fortress. The army that clears Utgard ends the age.

rules.fullBattles: Every endgame fight is a full battle: the loser loses everything, the winner loses a share that grows the closer the fight was. There is no raid cap here.
rules.towers: Each wasted island with Utgard has three to six jötun watchtowers spread over it, and Utgard itself, each with a jötunn garrison.
rules.assault: Send an army to assault a watchtower or Utgard. The jötnar you kill stay dead; the garrison only regrows slowly, so a guild can wear it down over several attacks.
rules.grace: A watchtower with no jötnar left is taken: it goes quiet and stays empty for 1 hour, then the garrison starts to regrow.
rules.holding: An army standing on a site holds it. Every hour the jötnar that regrew come out and fight it in a full battle. While the army wins, the site stays down.
rules.loot: A holding army takes loot every hour (300 at a watchtower, 1,000 at Utgard: 40% iron, 30% food, 30% stone) until its carry capacity is full. What it cannot carry is lost.
rules.aggression: Sites with jötnar ambush armies that come into their guard range and burn player towers inside it unless an army defends them. After a fight a site is calm for 1 hour.
rules.walls: Utgard stands inside one or two rings of walls, if the island has room: the inner ring at level 2, the outer one at level 1. They block land armies, and their gates never open for players.
rules.breaching: Walls are broken with the siege mission: bring catapults or rams, march next to a wall hex and strike. At level 0 the wall is breached and armies can pass.
rules.wallPace: An Utgard wall loses at most one level a day, and repairs one level a day while no army stands on or next to it. The inner ring needs two strikes a day apart, with an army kept beside it in between.
rules.ram: The ram is a second siege engine: the same siege power as the catapult, much tougher, but slower.
rules.gateRule: Utgard can only be assaulted while every watchtower on its island is taken. Keep armies on the towers, or they regrow and Utgard's gate stays shut.
rules.winning: The army that leaves Utgard with no jötnar wins the age. The player who threw it down is recorded as the conqueror, and every member of their guild gets the guild win.
rules.ageEnd: Depending on the world, the age then ends and the world turns read-only, or play goes on with the winner announced.

island.heading: Living and wasted, side by side
island.body: Wasted islands are born wasted: they rise from the sea as they are, and no living island ever turns. This made-up island is only a toy for comparing the two tile sets. Drag the slider to swap its living tiles for their wasted counterparts, ring by ring from the centre out.
island.hoverHint: Point at a hex to see what it is.

pairs.heading: Living and wasted
pairs.body: Every wasted tile has a living counterpart of the same shape, so rivers, coasts and mountain feet line up the same way on both kinds of island.

grass.lore: Ash-mottled basalt. It can be rubble, obsidian shards, a rune-lit fissure, a web of lava cracks or a smoking vent.

forest.lore: A snag stands where each tree stood. They are bleached, grey or charred, and a third of them have snapped off.

sand.lore: Volcanic grit, scattered with pebbles of the same stone.

mountain.lore: Slim spires of dark rock with ash on their crests. Nothing grows on them.

river.lore: The same channel as a river, running with fire instead of water. Where one rises, lava wells up from a small cone of its own.

sea.lore: Green-black water over a dark seabed.

coast.lore: Shallows over black sand. Here lie the wreck of a longship, a basalt rock and a reef of obsidian spikes.

wildlifeCamps.title: Wildlife camps
wildlifeCamps.intro: Unclaimed islands are not empty. Wolves, bears, seals and worse hold them, each pack in a camp of its own. You may land and settle, but a strong camp burns down any tower near it that no army guards, so on a big island you clear the camps in your way and build where the land is free.
wildlifeCamps.status: Camps are alive: you can hunt them, they regrow, and strong camps fight back. The rules below are the ones the game plays by; the bog camps (moose mire, beaver lodge, crane dance) stand on plain bog moss.

rules.heading: How a camp works
rules.towers: A guarded camp holds the land around it. Strong camps attack: a tower inside the range of an aggressive strong camp is burned down unless one of your armies stands guard on it. The game warns you when you place one. Beyond the range the island is open to build on.
rules.range: How far a camp reaches depends on its level, which is rolled at random when the camp appears. A strong camp can hold a wide stretch of land; a weak one only its nearest hexes.
rules.bigIslands: A small island may be held entirely by one camp. On a big island you can clear just the camps in the way and put up towers where the land is then free.
rules.states: A camp has two states: guarded, with its beasts, and cleared (empty). A damaged camp regrows and still counts as guarded.
rules.building: Once a camp is cleared you can build on its hex (not Fenrir's brood), and the building removes the camp for as long as it stands.
rules.respawn: A cleared camp refills only while its hex lies outside every realm. An empty camp inside a realm stays empty; when the building on it is gone and the hex is outside every realm, the camp comes back.
rules.neverBuilt: The eagle's eyrie on its sea stack and Fenrir's brood in the wastes are never built on: the empty nest stays on the map, and Fenrir's brood keeps coming back.
rules.hunting: Hunting: send land units to a camp's hex with the Hunt order. Your army attack is fought against the beasts' defense, a tie goes to the camp. The loser loses everything, the winner part of its force. A win clears the camp and pays its loot.
rules.regrowth: Regrowth: a damaged camp regrows its beasts evenly over 4 hours (weak camps) or 8 hours (strong camps).
rules.calm: Calm: after any fight a camp is calm for 24 hours. It regrows but does not attack.
rules.leveling: Leveling: every 10th clear of a camp, by any player, raises its level by 1, up to 100. It never drops back. Its guard range stays as rolled, so a farmed camp gets tougher but does not claim more land.
rules.ambush: Ambush: a strong camp that is not calm and still has adults or alphas ambushes armies that enter its range. Beaten armies retreat home; either way the camp is calm for 24 hours.
rules.leftover: Leftover loot: what your army cannot carry stays at the camp for the next hunter. A hunt on a barely regrown camp pays little, and a hunt on an empty camp only picks up the leftover.

camps.heading: The camps
camps.body: Each kind of ground has its own camps, a strong one and sometimes a weak one. Filter them by strength or ground, switch a camp between guarded and cleared, and turn it through the six directions a tile can face.
camps.rotations: A guarded camp only has art for the directions that show its animals best; the other directions are greyed out, and on the map the camp is turned to one of those. A cleared camp can face any direction.

strength.label: Strength
strength.help: Strong camps roll high levels and hold a wide stretch of land; no new player lands near one. Weak camps roll low and hold only their nearest hexes: a new player's first, safe fights.

wildlifeCamps.range: Guards {min} to {max} hexes around it, by its level (1 to {levels}).

loot.label: Loot
loot.moreHint: A larger share of this than other camps pay
loot.note: Clearing a camp pays loot. Every camp gives food from the hunt and a strong camp adds iron, the gear of earlier settlers its pack has eaten; some camps add what their ground holds, and ++ marks a camp's biggest share (double weight). The pool grows with the camp's level, slower than its garrison, so an early clear pays far more than it costs.

wildlifeCamps.notKept: Guarded art only exists for the directions that show the animals best

wolfden.name: Wolf den
wolfden.guards: A wolf howling from the boulder crown, two wolves on the prowl and two pups.

bearrapids.name: Bear rapids
bearrapids.guards: A bear fishing from a boulder in the river, a bear and a cub on the north bank, another cub across the water.

sealhaulout.name: Seal haul-out
sealhaulout.guards: Five seals basking on the slabs and the sand, two heaving themselves along, and three white pups.

walrushaulout.name: Walrus haul-out
walrushaulout.guards: Walrus bulls with long tusks on the shore, one rearing up to fight, among the bones of their kills.
walrushaulout.artNote: Drawn with the seal art until its own is ready.

boarwallow.name: Boar wallow
boarwallow.guards: Two boars lying in the mud, one on patrol, and three striped piglets.

eagleeyrie.name: Eagle eyrie
eagleeyrie.guards: An eagle and two eaglets on a nest on top of a sea stack, while its mate circles overhead.

fenrirbrood.name: Fenrir's brood
fenrirbrood.guards: Black wolves with ember eyes on an ash floor: one on guard, two on the prowl, and two pups.

moosemire.name: Moose mire
moosemire.guards: A bull moose wading, a cow browsing and two calves.

beaverlodge.name: Beaver lodge
beaverlodge.guards: Two beavers swimming by the lodge and two more on the bank.

cranedance.name: Crane dance
cranedance.guards: A pair of cranes dancing, three standing, one walking, and a juvenile.

deerglade.name: Deer glade
deerglade.guards: A stag by the salt lick, two hinds grazing and a spotted fawn.

harewarren.name: Hare warren
harewarren.guards: Two hares sitting up on the warren mound, three bounding round it and one grazing.

otterslide.name: Otter slide
otterslide.guards: One otter swimming, one on the drift log with a fish, one running the bank and one waiting at the holt.

bogLands.title: Bog lands
bogLands.intro: Wet moss ground (Old Norse mýrr), cut by slow creeks and dark lakes. Rust-coloured seeps mark the bog iron that is dug here, and clay is cut from the lake shores. Bogs are part of the living lands and meet grass at a hex edge.
bogLands.status: Bogs now appear in worlds: a lake with a river running through it on most big islands, and a lake with a bog ring where an island encloses a pocket of sea. The bog buildings are in: the bog-ore works and the Clay Brickworks on plain bog, the Fishing Hut on a lake's half shore, and the Hammer Forge on a creek (with the river mill's art until it has its own).

example.heading: Example map
example.body: A small island the game itself generated, with its bog, creek and lake drawn exactly as a world draws them. Hover a hex to see what it is.
example.hoverHint: Point at a hex to see what it is.

ground.heading: Bog ground
ground.body: Moss ground in several looks, mixed across a bog. The ore seep and the seep chain are where bog iron shows at the surface.

water.heading: Creeks and bog lakes
water.body: Creeks flow into rivers; lakes are open water with shore tiles around them. All of them are water tiles.

creek.name: Creek
creek.body: A straight creek. Its looks add sedge banks or a reed bed.

creekBend.name: Creek bend
creekBend.body: A creek turning 120°. Creeks never turn sharper and never fork.

spring.name: Spring
spring.body: Where a creek begins: a round pool that wells up, ringed by pale stones.

lake.name: Lake
lake.body: Open water. Its looks add an islet, a floating moss mat, a reed island or a fish weir.

inlet.name: Inlet shore
inlet.body: A shore with one water edge; one look has a clay bank.

shore.name: Shore
shore.body: A shore with two water edges; one look has a clay bank.

half.name: Half shore
half.body: A shore with three water edges, where the lake Fishing Hut stands.

mouth.name: Creek mouth
mouth.body: Where a creek runs into a lake, arriving opposite the inlet's water edge.

buildings.heading: Buildings on the bog
buildings.body: Four buildings belong to the bog. Step through the stages each one grows through as it is built up.

bogoreworks.name: Bog-ore works
bogoreworks.body: The iron producer, on plain bog moss: from a few diggings in the seeps to a bloomery smelting the ore. Every bog, creek or lake tile next to it adds to its output.

fisherhut.name: Fishing Hut (lake)
fisherhut.body: The Fishing Hut, on stilts over a bog-lake shore (a half shore). The same building as the coastal one, with its own art; it counts the lake tiles around it the way the coastal hut counts sea.

hammerschmiede.name: Hammer Forge
hammerschmiede.body: A water-powered hammer mill on a bog creek, behind a level-10 bog-ore works: it raises every bog-ore works within its range.
hammerschmiede.artNote: Shown with the river hammer mill's art until it gets art of its own.

claybrickworks.name: Clay Brickworks
claybrickworks.body: Clay dug from the bog and fired into bricks: a new player's first source of stone. It stands on plain bog moss instead of grass.

rules.heading: How bogs are laid out
rules.body: The bog tiles only fit together in certain ways, so the map follows a few rules:
rules.waterEdges: A bog tile touches at most three water tiles, and they are next to each other.
rules.lakesApart: Separate lakes are at least two tiles apart.
rules.creeks: Creeks run straight or bend 120°, and end in a spring or a lake mouth.
rules.mouth: A creek meets a lake only at a mouth.
rules.weir: The fish weir only appears near a lake Fishing Hut.
rules.boats: Boats appear on a lake only where a lake Fishing Hut or a bog-ore works stands beside it, and not for every building: each one has an even chance, a small lake holds one boat at most, a big lake one per twelve water tiles, and boats and weirs keep three tiles apart.
rules.landing: Every landing spot offered to a new player has bog in reach, because the Clay Brickworks and the bog-ore works both need it.
rules.river: A river always runs through the lake: it enters by one creek mouth and leaves by another. Now and then a second river is sunk into the lake, or a creek spring in the bog starts a river of its own.
rules.inland: Bog never touches the sea or the beach. Where an island wraps around a pocket of sea, that pocket becomes a bog lake with a ring of bog, and the rivers nearby run into it.

paused.reducedMotion: Animations are paused because your device asks for reduced motion.
paused.saveData: Animations are paused because your browser is saving data.
paused.off: Animations are switched off on this device.

walls.title: Walls
walls.intro: The palisade is the earth-and-timber wall of the Viking age, and above all a movement barrier: it stops land armies, not boats. It unlocks at Longhouse 7, behind a level-5 Tower, and has 3 levels. Each wall hex costs about 40 wood and 10 stone at level 1.

pieces.heading: The six pieces
pieces.body: A wall is built one hex at a time, and every hex draws one of six pieces. Each piece comes in six rotations and in every stage the art has, from the construction site to the finished wall. Each is drawn here the way the map draws it: the ground, with the piece on top.

straight.name: Straight
straight.body: The run of the wall: it joins two opposite neighbours.

bend60.name: 60° bend
bend60.body: The tight turn, between two adjacent neighbours. It only occurs in a triangle of three wall hexes, because a fourth hex would make the wall fork.

bend120.name: 120° bend
bend120.body: The wide turn, with one neighbour skipped: the wall changes direction by 60°.

gate.name: Gate
gate.body: A straight with a gate in the middle. It lets its owner's armies and their friends' through, and no one else's.

end.name: Land end
end.body: The last hex of a wall on land, with a single wall neighbour. It is half open: any army can cross it at a cost.

seaEnd.name: Sea end
seaEnd.body: Where a wall runs out into the water: it stands on coastal water, touches exactly one land wall hex, and has its own water ground.

choosing.heading: How the pieces are chosen
choosing.body: You only decide where a hex of wall goes. The game picks the piece and its rotation from the wall hexes around it, and picks again when a neighbour is added or removed, so an end turns into a straight when the wall grows past it.

rules.fork: Walls never fork: no hex may have three or more wall neighbours.
rules.gate: A gate only fits on a straight, with a wall hex on two opposite sides, and that has to stay true after any later placement.
rules.sea: A sea end touches exactly one land wall hex and can never be a gate.

choosing.example: An example: a wall that ends on land, runs straight, passes a gate, runs on, turns by 120° and runs out into the sea. The game worked out each piece and its rotation from the hexes alone.

example.alt: An example wall of {count} hexes on grass, ending in the sea.

where.heading: Where walls can stand
where.body: On grass, forest, sand and plain bog moss, inside your territory. The wall keeps the ground it stands on: on forest the trees are cleared and the forest floor stays. Walls cannot be built on rivers, streams, mountains, bog water or lakes. The sea end is the exception that proves it: it stands on coastal water.

movement.heading: Movement
movement.body: Walls are about land armies. Fleets are not affected.

rules.block: A wall hex blocks every land army, your own included. Only standing hexes count: a construction site does not block.
rules.gate: A gate lets the owner's armies through, and those of the owner's guild and of guilds at peace with it, as quickly as the ground under it. Everyone else is stopped.
rules.end: A land end is half open: any army can cross it, but the step costs 3 more than the ground under it, so armies only take it when there is no open way round. If it touches a mountain or a wide river it is a sealed end and blocks like any wall hex.
rules.sea: A wall that ends in the sea end seals at the coast. A wall that merely stops on land next to open sea does not: its half-open end is the way through.
rules.natural: Land armies cannot cross mountains at all, and wide rivers only over a bridge. A wall run up to either one is sealed there anyway, bridge or not.
rules.rivers: Rivers: a wide river is no way through for a land army unless a bridge spans it, but a wall that ends at one is sealed there either way. A stream is shallow enough to wade, and no wall can be built in running water, so a stream is always a way through: slow, but open. A wall that ends at a stream is not sealed there. Walls cannot stand on either.
rules.fleets: Fleets are not affected by walls.

diagram.sealed: A wall run up to mountains on both ends: no way through.
diagram.riverEnd: A wall run up to a wide river is sealed there, just like at a mountain, with or without a bridge on the river.
diagram.halfOpen: A wall that simply stops on land: any army crosses its last hex, but the step costs 3 more than the ground under it.
diagram.stream: No wall can be built in a stream, and any army can wade it, which costs even more than the wall's end. So a stream is always a gap in the wall, and the end next to it stays half open.
diagram.seaEnd: The line runs out into the water on a sea end: sealed at the coast.
diagram.gate: A gate is a gap between two posts. It opens for its owner and the owner's friends: the same guild, or guilds at peace.

notBuilt.heading: Not built yet
notBuilt.body: Fire taking a level off a wall: a wall will lose its levels one at a time until it is gone. Nothing burns walls yet. Sieges already do this: see the siege section above.

sieges.heading: Sieges
sieges.body: A wall can be breached, one level at a time. Only catapults do it, and only as part of an attack on the settlement the wall belongs to.

rules.who: Send an attack (or a raid) with catapults at the settlement and name the wall hex as the target when you send it. If your army wins the battle, the catapults that survived fire at that hex. One surviving catapult is enough; an army that loses the battle fires nothing.
rules.target: If you name no target, or the building you named is gone by the time your army arrives, the siege hits a random building of that settlement instead, a wall hex among them.
rules.level: A won siege takes exactly one level off a wall hex, the gate included, however many catapults survive. Most buildings lose several levels at once to a strong army; a wall is breached a level at a time. A palisade or gate has {levels} levels, so a fully built wall hex takes {levels} won sieges. A damaged wall still stops armies until its last level is gone.
rules.gone: At level 0 the wall hex is gone: its hex is free ground again and armies walk through it. Any build order still queued for that hex is dropped.
rules.rebuild: The owner can raise a wall hex that is still standing by a level again, like any building, and can build on a hex that is gone again under the usual placement rules. There is no separate repair.

production.title: Resource production
production.intro: Where wood, stone, food and iron come from, and how mills raise them.

producers.heading: Producers
producers.growth: A producer's output grows by 20% with every level: each level makes 1.2 times what the one before made.
producers.perHour: All figures are per hour, before any boost from neighbours, mills or shrines.

notes.pumpkinfarm: Only on an island with pumpkin soil
notes.fishinghut: or on the half shore of a bog lake
notes.bogoreworks: Plain bog moss only, not shore, creek or lake

producers.longhouse: The Longhouse is the exception: it adds the same fixed amount every level ({amounts} an hour: wood / stone / food / iron) instead of growing by 20%.
producers.soil: Every island has either wheat or pumpkin soil, about half of them each. A {pumpkin} fits only pumpkin soil and makes {pumpkinRate} food at level 1 where a {farm} makes {farmRate}; a {farm} fits any island.

boost.heading: Neighbour boost
boost.body: Each of the six hexes around a producer that matches adds {per}% to its output, up to {max}% (five matching hexes). What counts as matching depends on the building.
boost.none: The {herder}, {farm}, {pumpkin} and {brickworks} get no neighbour boost.

mills.heading: Mills
mills.body: A mill makes nothing itself. It raises every building of its kind within reach by 5% per level: 50% at level 10 and 100% at level {max}. Its reach starts at one ring, the six hexes around it, and grows by one ring every four levels. Several mills add up.
mills.notPumpkin: The {crop} raises Farms only; a {pumpkin} gets nothing from it.

storage.heading: Storage
storage.body: Each resource stops growing at your storage limit, and nothing above it is kept. With no storage building the limit is {base} of each resource. These buildings raise it.
storage.levelCap: A {storehouse} or {great} cannot be higher than your {longhouse}.
storage.moreBody: You can build more than one Storehouse, but each extra one asks for more of the ones you already have.

step.needsCell: {count} storehouse at level {level} | {count} storehouses at level {level}

storage.overCap: A cost above your storage limit can never be paid, however long you wait. Build storage before an upgrade that costs more than you can hold.

upkeep.heading: Upkeep and shrines
upkeep.body: Troops eat food every hour. When your food runs out, units starve, the ones that cost the most to feed first, until your food income is no longer negative. Armies on the road have their own food rules: see {movement}.
upkeep.shrines: Two shrines raise production: {freyja} adds to food, {ullr} to wood. See {shrines} for everything the gods give.

adminNote.tooltips: The production figures in tooltips and the build menu include the neighbour boost but not mills or shrines. The tables on this page show the base figures.

founding.title: Founding settlements
founding.intro: Settler troops from the cart workshop, and where a new settlement can land.

first.heading: Your first settlement
first.body: You pick your first settlement from a few starting spots the game offers you. Each one is on grassland near forest, away from the sea, with bog within reach for clay and iron, and clear of strong wildlife camps and giants.

more.heading: More settlements
more.body: Further settlements are founded by {count} Settler crews marching together. You train them at the {workshop}, which needs a {longhouse} of level {level} and a {square} of level {squareLevel}.
more.provisions: Each crew carries {food} food, {total} for all three. Load enough for the way there and back.
more.ambush: On the way, overland crews can be ambushed by strong wildlife camps (see {camps}). How fast they cross each ground is on the {movement} page.

renown.heading: Renown and price
renown.body: Every settlement after the first has a price in renown and in crews. Your buildings earn renown in all your settlements together: 1 per building level per hour, and it never decays. Each settlement you hold doubles the renown asked for the next one and the price of its crews.
renown.when: The renown is checked when the crews set out.
renown.feasts: A feast at the {square} earns renown on top of that. It runs {hours} hours, costs the same amount of wood, stone and food, and grows with the square's level.

where.heading: Where a settlement can land
where.land: On any land hex your crews can reach, except a giant's.
where.spacing: At least {hexes} hexes beyond the claim border of every settlement in the world, yours and other players'.
where.twice: This is checked when the crews set out and again when they arrive.
where.taken: If someone else took the spot meanwhile, the crews wait there. You can send them on or recall them, and they head home on their own when their food runs low.

new.heading: A new settlement
new.body: It starts with a level 1 {longhouse}. Its claim reaches {claim1} hexes, {claim2} from level 2, and its stores hold {stock} each of wood, stone and food, and no iron.
new.garrison: Every unit that travelled with the crews, other than the crews themselves, stays as its garrison.

adminNote.sea: Founding by sea exists in the rules but has no interface yet (issue #447).
adminNote.provisions: The expansion panel proposes 200 provisions by default, but three crews carry only {carried}.

landMovement.title: Land movement
landMovement.intro: How armies cross the land: ground costs, rivers, mountains and walls.

cost.heading: What a hex costs
cost.body: Every hex an army enters has a cost set by its ground. An army needs the cost divided by its speed, in hours, to cross the hex, so a hex of cost 2 takes twice as long as grass.
cost.streamNote: flat, whatever ground it runs over
cost.walls: A wall hex stops every land army, and a gate lets friends through. See {walls} for the full rules.

pace.heading: How fast armies move
pace.body: Speed is counted in hexes per hour on grass. An army marches at the speed of its slowest unit.
pace.start: Your troops set out from the building that trained them and return there. An army of several unit types leaves from the building of its slowest unit.
pace.example: Example: a {unit} crosses a grass hex in {minutes}.
pace.note: Time per hex at the default world speed. A faster world shortens every time.
pace.slowest: The slowest of all is the {unit}.

food.heading: Food on the march
food.upkeep: An army eats its units' upkeep in food every hour from the moment it sets out.
food.carry: It can carry only as much food as its units can, so you load the provisions for the whole trip before it leaves.
food.turnBack: An army on a move turns back when its food runs low.

road.heading: On the road
road.camps: An army that comes within reach of a strong wildlife camp is ambushed, unless the camp is calm. A strong camp guards {min} to {max} hexes around it (2 plus its level). See {link}.
road.enemies: Hostile armies that meet on the road fight a field battle. Armies of the same owner or guild never fight each other.
road.orders: Every order has one destination for free. Waypoints along the way are a premium feature.

sight.heading: What an army sees
sight.body: A travelling army uncovers {rings} rings of the map around it, plus {bonus} more for each level of the {odin}.

bridges.heading: Bridges over wide rivers
bridges.body: A wide river is no way through for a land army, unless a {bridge} spans it. You build it on the river hex itself, inside your claim, from Longhouse {longhouse} behind a level-{level} {townsquare}. Costs and build times of every level are in the tech tree.
bridges.friends: Its owner’s armies and their friends’: the same guild, or a guild at peace with it. Every other army is stopped as if there were no bridge.

rules.where: A bridge fits on a straight or bending wide river hex, whatever ground lies under it. It does not fit on a spring, a fork or a mouth, on a stream (armies wade streams anyway) or on a wasted island.
rules.site: A building site does not open the river. Only a finished bridge, level 1 or more, counts. Each level makes the crossing quicker, up to the king’s bridge, where armies cross as fast as over the ground itself.
rules.guarded: The guarded bridge works like a wall gate: it lets through its owner’s armies and their friends’ and stops everyone else.
rules.siege: Catapults can burn a bridge down, one level per won siege, however many catapults survive. A guarded bridge therefore falls to the king’s bridge first and is then open to everyone, attackers included. A causeway burnt down once is gone, and the river is shut again.
rules.walls: A bridge does not change walls: a wall that runs up to a wide river is sealed there, with or without a bridge. See {walls}.
rules.fleets: Bridges matter only to land armies. Ships are not affected.

ships.title: Ships and water
ships.intro: Ships from the dockyard, fleets at sea, and what walls cannot stop.

dockyard.heading: The dockyard
dockyard.body: Ships are trained at the {dockyard}, which needs a {longhouse} of level {level} and a {hut} of level {hutLevel}.
dockyard.shore: It stands on shallow (coastal) water, so only a settlement that holds shoreline can train ships.

sailing.heading: At sea
sailing.sea: Ships sail on the sea only. Coastal and open water cost the same, and bog lakes are closed to them.
sailing.troops: Ships carry loot, not land troops.
sailing.targets: A fleet can attack, raid or support settlements that hold shoreline. It cannot take catapults along.
sailing.camps: Wildlife camps never ambush a fleet (see {camps}).

battles.heading: Battles
battles.same: Fleets fight by the same rules as armies on land: attack against defence, and a tie goes to the defender.
battles.tower: A defending settlement's {tower} adds {percent}% defence per level.
battles.njord: The {shrine} raises your ships' attack by {low}% at level 1, up to {high}% at level 5. See {shrines}.

adminNote.route: Known gap (issue #450): a fleet cannot yet attack or raid a settlement whose centre is inland, even when that settlement's land reaches the shore.
adminNote.sea: Founding by sea (a Karve carries {karve} Settler crew, a Longship {longship}) exists in the rules but has no interface yet (issue #447).

shrines.title: Shrines
shrines.intro: A shrine wins you a god's favour: a lasting bonus for the whole settlement. You get one shrine per settlement, so the choice matters.

rules.heading: The rules
rules.oneShrine: A settlement can hold one shrine in total, of any god. Odin's statue counts as a shrine.
rules.oneGod: Each god can have only one shrine on an island, whichever settlement raises it first.
rules.needs: Every shrine needs a {longhouse} of level {level} and the building listed for its god in the table below. A shrine can be raised to level {max}.

gods.heading: What each god gives

favour.odin: Every build finishes sooner, and you see farther.

gods.costs: Costs and build times of every level are in the {link}.

runes.heading: Runes
runes.body: A shrine's level opens rune slots. Each slotted rune adds its own bonus on top of the god's favour.
runes.cap: Shrines and runes add up, but any one kind of bonus stops at +{percent}%.
